title: Readmitted to England
hookLine: Menasseh ben Israel petitions Cromwell, and Jews quietly return

cards: A few weeks ago on this path, a king ordered every Jew out of England. Homes emptied. A London street kept only the name, Old Jewry.

Now a rabbi from Amsterdam is crossing the North Sea with a petition in his bag. He is a teacher, a writer and a printer, with a big hope and a practical request for England's ruler, Oliver Cromwell: may we come back?

teach.b: His name was Menasseh ben Israel, from the Amsterdam community we met two days ago, and he carried two kinds of reasons.

teach.h: A HOPE AND A PRACTICAL REQUEST.
teach.b: One was a hope. The Torah speaks of Israel scattered from one end of the earth to the other, and Menasseh wrote that the redemption would come once the scattering was complete.
If Jews could live in England too, he believed, that day would come nearer. The other reason was plainer: Jews needed safe places to live, and they could bring trade and skill.
He addressed Cromwell in writing, and later answered the old lies about Jews in a pamphlet of his own.
Cromwell called a conference in London. Merchants, lawyers and clergy argued: some for admitting Jews, some for strict conditions, some for no admission at all. It ended without a formal decision.
No law was passed, and Menasseh was left disappointed. But something quieter happened. A small group of Jews was already living in London, outwardly as Spanish and Portuguese Catholic merchants.
They asked to pray together in private and to bury their dead, and they were allowed to. They rented a house for a synagogue and found land for a cemetery.
That is what readmitted looks like here: not a ceremony, but a door left unlocked, and people walking through it carefully.
This week: a tablecloth over a code of law, the lion of Safed, Lecha Dodi, the ghetto, Amsterdam, Spinoza, and now a shut door opening a crack.

how: Jewish communities in Britain trace their modern history to this quiet return, and the Spanish and Portuguese congregation in London still keeps the customs of the families who came back.

games.q: you are Cromwell. merchants, lawyers and clergy have argued for days about letting Jews return. what do you do?
o: pass a law readmitting the Jews with full rights.
order the Jews in London to leave.
end the meeting without a formal decision.
games.why: no law was passed. but the Jews already in London were quietly allowed to pray and bury their dead: readmitted without a ceremony.

practice: Think of one door in your life that is closed: a relationship, a place, a chance you want. Menasseh made his case in writing, plainly; shape yours in one or two sentences in your mind, and just find the words.
If you pray, you can bring that request in your own words.

wordCard.voice: Menasseh. The Amsterdam rabbi who petitioned Oliver Cromwell to let Jews return to England, and watched a door open quietly instead of by law. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: readmitted. Sometimes a door opens by a crack, not by a law. That's the week, day nine hundred fifty-nine.
